claim: Beam-transfer parameter between two apertures: tau = sqrt(A_t A_r)/(lambda D); efficiency curve vs tau for optimum (Gaussian-tapered) illumination credited to Goubau (J. Microwave Power 5(4), 1970)
locator: W. C. Brown (Raytheon), NASA-CR-103090 / PT-2931 final report, Sec. 3.3.2, report p. 54 (PDF p. 63), Fig. 3-17 'Microwave Power Transfer Efficiency Between Transmitting and Receiving Apertures'; ref. 28 = Goubau 1970
quote: we find the relationship between the efficiency, aperture areas, distance of transmission, and wavelength of the radiation given in Figure 3-17. The horizontal parameter in Figure 3-17 is √(AtAr)/λD
notes: The formula token after 'is' is typeset as an image; transcribed from the rendered page. Symbols defined on the same page: At transmitting aperture area, Ar receiving aperture area, λ wavelength, D separation. Fig. 3-17 is a curve (circular and quadratic apertures), not a closed form; by eye it reads ~60% at tau=1 and ~98% at tau=2, consistent with 1-exp(-tau^2) (not digitized). Primary Goubau 1970 (Taylor & Francis) and Brown & Eves 1992 (IEEE MTT 40(6)) not retrieved: paywalled.

claim: Closed-form beam efficiency between two apertures: eta = 1 - exp(-tau^2), tau^2 = A_t A_r/(lambda D)^2
locator: N. Shinohara, J. Korean Inst. Electromagn. Eng. Sci. 10(4):224-230 (Dec 2010), p. 225, Eqs. (2)-(3) and the paragraph after Fig. 1; attributed to ref. [1] = W. C. Brown, IEEE Trans. MTT 40(6):1239-1250, 1992
quote: τ² = AtAr/(λD)² (2) η = Pr/Pt = 1 − e^(−τ²) (3) ... The equation (3) is approximation. We can calculate the BE exactly with calculation of near field beam pattern.
notes: Equations transcribed from the rendered page (text layer garbles superscripts). DOI 10.5515/JKIEES.2010.10.4.224. Secondary source for the closed form (the author is a leading WPT researcher, Kyoto RISH); it cites Brown 1992 rather than Goubau. The paper states it is an approximation (optimal Gaussian-type taper), so use it as the ideal upper envelope, not an exact result.

claim: URSI SPS white paper: transfer efficiency approaches 100% for tau > 2 with Gaussian aperture distributions, tau = A/(lambda D) with A the geometric mean of A_t and A_r (= sqrt(A_t A_r))
locator: URSI White Paper on SPS and Report of the URSI ICWG on SPS (June 2007), Sec. 3.1.1, report p. 120 (PDF p. 141); refs 1 = Brown 1992, 2 = Goubau & Schwering 1961
quote: Brown1 showed that the power transmission efficiency can approach 100% if parameter τ=A/(λD) is larger than 2 and the distributions on the aperture are Gaussian, where A is the geometric mean of the transmitter and receiver aperture areas
notes: Independent (international scientific union) statement of the same tau definition: A = sqrt(At*Ar) makes A/(lambda D) identical to the Brown/Goubau tau.

claim: URSI SPS white paper worked point: efficiency at tau = 2.4 (Brown's optimum-taper curve)

claim: A universal N x N multiport interferometer (any unitary) needs N(N-1)/2 variable beam splitters in both the Reck and the Clements (rectangular) mesh
locator: Clements et al., arXiv:1603.08788v2 (8 Feb 2017), Fig. 1 caption, PDF p. 2; published as Optica 3(12):1460 (2016)
quote: A universal N-mode multiport interferometer ... can be implemented using a mesh of N(N − 1)/2 beam splitters such as a) the one proposed by Reck or b) the one that we demonstrate in this paper.

claim: Each variable beam splitter in the Clements mesh is one MZI (two 50:50 couplers + phase shift); the mesh has optical depth N (Reck: 2N-3)
value: 1 MZI per beam splitter; depth N
locator: Clements et al., arXiv v2, Fig. 1 caption (PDF p. 2); depth statement main text PDF p. 3
quote: crossings between two modes correspond to a variable beam splitter described by a Tm,n (θ, φ) matrix, which can be implemented by a Mach-Zehnder interferometer consisting of two 50:50 directional couplers
notes: Depth, p. 3: 'the Reck design has an optical depth of 2N −3, whereas our design has an optical depth of N'. With DERIVATIONS' column count (N/2 columns of N/2 MZIs + N/2 columns of N/2-1) this gives N(N-1)/2.

claim: Photoelectric multiplication: inputs are time-encoded and each balanced homodyne detector integrates charge Q_i proportional to sum_j A_ij x_j (a full dot product per detector read)
locator: Hamerly et al., Phys. Rev. X 9, 021032 (2019); arXiv:1812.07614v2 p. 3, paragraph before Eq. (2)
quote: Input (output) data are encoded temporally as N (N′) pulses on a single channel ... each detector functions as a quantum photoelectric multiplier, calculating the homodyne product between the two signals
notes: Supports DERIVATIONS E015 (time-integration correction): one detector read accumulates the N time-sequential products. PRX is CC BY 4.0 (Crossref license field); quote from arXiv v2 (18 May 2019).

claim: Standard quantum limit (shot noise) per MAC for homodyne optical neural networks, MNIST benchmarks
value: 0.5-1 aJ (5-10 photons) at N=100; 50-100 zJ (0.5-1 photon) at N=1000
locator: Hamerly et al. PRX 9, 021032 (2019); arXiv v2 p. 4, section 'Deep Learning at the Standard Quantum Limit', Fig. 2(c) discussion
quote: This is around 0.5–1 aJ (5–10 photons) for the small network (inner layer size N = 100), and 50–100 zJ (0.5–1 photon) for the large network (inner layer size N = 1000).
notes: Simulated bound (network-dependent); abstract: 'This bound, which can be as low as 50 zJ/MAC'. Same page: SNR scales as n_mac. Overlaps R8-001 / R7-007; this row adds the per-detector statement pairing in the next row.

claim: Per-detector photon number under photoelectric multiplication = N * n_mac, typically >> 1 even when n_mac < 1
locator: Hamerly et al. PRX 9, 021032 (2019); arXiv v2 p. 4, parenthetical after the SQL values
quote: (Note that this is per MAC, the number of photons per detector N n_mac is typically ≫ 1.)
notes: '≫' confirmed on the rendered page (text layer drops it); subscript written as n_mac. This is the paper's own statement that the shot-noise budget is set per integrated read (N MACs), which is the E015 argument; energy per MAC = per-read energy / N.
